speechtext: MR. MacINNIS (CAPE BRETON-EAST RICHMOND)-POSITION OF CAPE BRETON DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION ON BENEFITS FOR FORMER EMPLOYEES

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege affecting the rights and prerogatives of parliamentary committees and one which reflects on the word of two ministers of the Crown.
First, the Cape Breton Development Corporation has constantly suggested, as in a release dated May 29, 1973, that the matter of the benefits for former Devco employees is "a matter of negotiation between the corporation and the union". There is no one union involved. The present Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) arranged for a delegation of five former Devco employees to appear before the regional development committee at public expense, representing former Devco employees but not constituting or representing any one union. The former minister stated in the House on January 29, 1970 that the group involved was "a small group of superannuated employees", and that they had no connection with the United Mine Workers of America who had made no request in the name of those pensioners.
Devco has attempted to contradict both the present and the former minister, and has put forward the illusion that they have things well in hand. In addition to this distortion of the situation perpetuated by Devco, the corporation has insinuated that the committee is interfering in the legitimate bargaining process by investigating the inadequacy and illegality of the pre-retirement benefits paid by Devco. As the chairman of the committee stated in a letter to Mr. Kent, the committees "are not answerable to government departments or agencies".
This question of the supremacy of parliament and its committees over government bureaucracies, and the obligation of agencies accurately to describe the situation, must be settled once and for all, Mr. Speaker. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. Muir):
That the matter of the affront of the Cape Breton Development Corporation and its president to the Standing Committee on Regional Development, and to two ministers of the Crown, be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that I have sent a copy of this to the chairman of the committee and to the two ministers involved.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member has provided the Chair with the required notice of his intention to raise this matter today by way of a question of privilege. The hon.
member appreciates that what he is proposing now is that this motion be given priority over all other business now before the House of Commons and that a debate ensue on the suggested question of privilege.
I would hesitate very much to suggest to the hon. member that the grievance he has should be debated by the House at this time by way of a question of privilege. Perhaps he would allow the Chair to look at the matter within the next few hours and to study the notes the hon. member has submitted to the Chair for consideration before reaching a decision whether there is a prima facie case of privilege that would justify the putting of the motion proposed by the hon. member and a debate based on the hon. member's motion. Again I ask that he give the Chair an opportunity to look into the matter on his behalf and on behalf of all other members of the House.

not the policy of the RCMP to publicly divulge the names and/or details of investigations conducted in the pursuit of its responsibilities. Such a policy is aimed at not only protecting the rights of the persons concerned, but also ensuring that any inquiries or investigations are not jeopardized through unnecessary public release. However, the RCMP responsibilities in the spheres of security screening, counter-subversion, counter-espionage, and the protection of VIPs necessitates contact with various elements of Canadian society, including the mass media. Such contact can take the form of either a thorough and detailed investigation, or, it may involve the clarification of a lead arising out of another investigation. In the latter instance, the Security Service is obligated to follow up such leads to determine if they have any substances. Sometimes this can only be resolved through an inquiry with a responsible person, such as the individual's supervisor, a fellow employee or some other person who may have knowledge of the individual concerned. When such an inquiry is made, the individual contacted is under no obligation to render assistance. Furthermore, for the reasons mentioned previously, it is hoped that the person contacted will respect the confidentiality of the inquiry. If such an inquiry shows that there is substance to the lead, then further investigation is undertaken to acquire all the relevant details necessary to take whatever action may be required as dictated by the circumstances. Should the opposite be the case, then no further action is taken. Such procedure is standard whether the inquiry is of a criminal or a security nature and, as such varies little from the procedures utilized by members of the media itself when pursuing a potential news story. The undertaking of any inquiry is not an indication that the Security Service is singling out for investigation any specific individual or group.

Federal Business Dex'elopment Bank FEDERAL BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT BANK ACT
May 6, 1974

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR INCORPORATION, OBJECTS, REGIONAL ADVISORY COUNCILS, POWERS

speechtext: The House resumed, from Friday, April 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gray (for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce) that Bill C-20, to incorporate the Federal Business Development Bank, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR INCORPORATION, OBJECTS, REGIONAL ADVISORY COUNCILS, POWERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is some while ago, April 26, that we were speaking on this bill and when I called it four o'clock the House moved to the private members' hour. With your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, if I may I should like to review for a moment the main points I was making that afternoon.
I expressed concern that the share of the national income attributed to small business has declined 3 per cent over the period 1962 to 1973. I made the point that it was a gradual decline, or an erosion of income of the small business sector of our economy over the span of 11 years. I made the point also that it was an extremely serious matter because the small businesses of this country contribute more than 50 per cent of the gross national product, pay more than 50 per cent of the taxes to the government treasury, and employ over 60 per cent of the labour force. I went on to say that any erosion of that base will have a far-reaching and long-lasting effect on our economy and our employment pattern.
I suggested as well that I would like to see the minister have Statistics Canada bring samples of all forms they send to small businesses to the Standing Committee on Industry, Trade and Commerce, and justify both the forms and the need to send them to these business people. I further requested that any new forms be cleared by the standing committee before they are sent out to small businessmen because the paper mountain they have to climb is getting beyond all reason.
I touched as well on the heavy handed approach to collateral being taken by the Industrial Development Bank, and expressed the hope that the new Federal Business Development Bank will, in fact, take a different approach and not leave this millstone around the neck of the small entrepreneur.
Then, finally, I made the point that we need a comprehensive approach to the problems facing the small businessman, that the new Federal Business Development Bank was a splint to the small business community and that the amendments to the Small Businesses Loans Act could be called a sling. What we really must do is go beyond Bill C-20 and Bill C-14, then look back to Bill C-259, and bring in the amendments promised by the then Minister of Finance, Mr. Benson, when this bill was passed through the House in 1971.
I feel the clauses of this bill dealing with the small business community must be simplified and written in a language that will be understood by the average businessman and his accountant. Small business people just do not have the resources to employ tax experts, and they are frustrated in their efforts to expand and improve their businesses because of this cloud over their heads. Of

course, to parallel any changes in Bill C-259 we should have a new and simplified tax form for small businessmen from the Department of National Revenue.
I suggest to you that the long-term success of the Federal Business Development Bank depends on whether the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) is able to convince his colleagues in the finance and national revenue portfolios that these changes must be made. Those were the main points, I believe, I made on the afternoon of April 26 when we suspended the debate on this bill and went into the private members' hour. It is difficult when we have these delays to pick up the thread of thought, but I will press on.
The Federal Business Development Bank can really breathe life back into this vital part cf our economy, the small business sector. We should really recognize the contribution that small businesses make to the economy of Canada. Small businesses provide a productive outlet for the energies of that large group of enterprising and independent people who attach great value to economic independence, many of whom may be less suited to employment in a large organization, but who have much to contribute to the vitality of our economy because of their independent, enterprising and individual thinking.
In industries where the optimum size of the production unit or the sales outlet is small, often the most efficient form of business organization is a small business. For this reason many important trades and industries consist mainly of small businesses. Many small businesses act as specialist suppliers to large companies of parts or subassemblies or components produced at lower costs than the larger companies could achieve. I think it is rather significant to note here that General Motors, in its North American operations, uses something of the order of 26,000 small businesses as suppliers that in fact employ less than 50 people in their operations.
Small businesses add greatly to the variety of products and services offered to the consumer because they can flourish in a limited or specialized market which would not in fact be worthwhile or economic for a large business to enter. In an economy in which ever larger multiproduct businesses are emerging, small businesses provide competition, both actual and potential, and provide some check on monopoly profits and on the inefficiency which monopoly breeds. In other words, they contribute to the efficient working of the economic system as a whole.
Small businesses, in spite of relatively low expenditure on research and development by that group as a whole, are an important source of innovation in products, techniques and services. The small business sector is the traditional breeding ground for new industry, and I think it is here that this new Federal Business Development Bank can do a great service through the service they are prepared to provide to the small businesses in counselling and the training of personnel to help them carry on.
I welcome this feature in the bill. I commend the minister for inserting it and expanding what I believe is the key program which I think is working quite well. I would caution the minister though to endeavour to bring into this organization small businessmen who have been sue-
May 6, 1974

cessful rather than retired vice-presidents of large corporations and expect them to advise the small businessmen. There are many cases, as I am sure the minister is aware, in which they do not speak the same language. Perhaps what is most important is that small business provides a means of entry into small business for new entrepreneurial talent, and is a seedbed from which new large companies will grow to challenge and stimulate the established leaders in much of our industry.
I should like to see this government adopt a Canada-first policy even at the expense of paying a premium for Canadian goods and services. I should like to see a loan policy adopted that the percentage of the loan would depend upon the percentage of Canadian ownership. That may be difficult to define, but I put forward the idea that this Federal Business Development Bank should, in fact, develop Canadian business for Canadians.
I sometimes find it difficult to reconcile the policies of this government as they pertain to DREE grants when I hear the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) say that there is no consultation with industry groups before establishing a new industry which, in fact, competes with existing Canadian enterprises. Would it not be more sane and sensible to consult with industry to determine if there is a desire to expand into an area that is lacking industry. On the one hand, we give a grant to a United States firm-this is an actual case-in the die-casting business to open a new venture in New Brunswick, where we know industry is needed, and find it is competing in the same United States export market with a wholly-owned Canadian company in another part of Canada. What is the rationale behind this? The minister says it is not departmental policy to cause this to happen, but it does happen.
So, I wonder where the Federal Business Development Bank fits into the DREE picture. Will we be able to stack loans from the Federal Business Development Bank, commercial sources and provincial agencies to provide the larger amounts of money required for some ventures? I think it is highly important that there be more liaison and co-operation, particularly between the provincial agencies and the Federal Business Development Bank. I know from personal experience that there is an attitude of competition between the two agencies. When one speaks to officials of either the federal IDB or the provincial agency, neither have very much that is good to say about the other. So, 1 would hope we would have a more comprehensive approach to this, and that we might look to the stacking of loans from various financial sources, some from the commercial side, some from provincial agencies and some from federal agencies.
I am sure, for example, that a Canadian automobile could be designed and marketed in Canada, but who would venture into such a field against the existing manufacturers. It just happens to be coincidental, but I noticed recently in the trade papers that there is a Japanese purchasing group in Canada endeavouring to purchase about 1,000 used trucks and spare parts for sale to mainland China in order to help that country mobilize a portion of its armed forces. These industry people tell me this will create a tremendous shortage of motor trucks in Canada. From looking at the production and consumption
Federal Business Development Bank figures in respect of new motor vehicles in Canada, I am confident that we could spawn an independent trucking industry in this country to the advantage of industry in general. We look ahead to projects such as the Mackenzie Valley pipeline, and if that project should get the go-ahead, the feeling among the people in the truck transport industry is that there will be a tremendous shortage of heavy duty vehicles in Canada.
I am sure there are people who are ready and willing to go into this field but you can appreciate I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that the stacking of loans to provide the necessary capital must be considered. I certainly hope the minister will look seriously at this proposal. I want to see the Federal Business Development Bank succeed. I want to see it become a vibrant agency removed from the rigidity of the bureaucracy of government. I want to see it inject into the small business community a new sense of direction and purpose. I want to see it revitalize the spirit of free enterprise which built this country. I want to see it respond to the talents we have in the communities. I believe in the person who has the courage to venture forth and accomplish his dreams, who takes his load of responsibility for the community and the nation squarely on his shoulders. I want to see the country shake off the socialist lethargy that is gradually creeping over us. I want to see direction given to the new people entering the business field by the removal of the iniquitous, complex and onerous tax system.
The complexities in respect of the tax system should be removed so that these people will be able to carry on their business in a more straightforward manner without being concerned about government regulations. I want to see a government in this country that will reaffirm its belief in the free enterprise system and say that it is not wrong to acquire and accumulate assets of value. I want to see a government that has the guts to stand up to the bureaucracy it has created, and which has the courage and wisdom to change it. This cannot happen if we merely put a band-aid here and a splint there. It must all be put together so that those people in our society who are carrying the greatest tax load, who are carrying the largest risk and who are employing the largest percentage of the work force will be stimulated to venture forth and seize the great opportunities there are before us. When this bill goes to the committee-when I put these thoughts together I did not anticipate that we would be looking at events as we are today with the possibility of an election-we will put some pretty hard questions to the minister. We will want to ask the minister about a Canada-first policy in respect of loans and purchasing. We will ask that he amend this bill so that the directors of the bank will be prohibited from borrowing from the new bank. I think that is a practice that should be eliminated.
I think we will want to press the minister to lay down guidelines regarding fees required when the small businessman desires a loan from the Federal Business Development Bank. Businessmen as a rule have their own lawyers. In the past, the IDB had a legal officer and, for some reason, required a third legal counsel-let us call him a patronage lawyer-to take part in the negotiations. In any case, the total legal fees on many loans from the

May 6, 1974
Federal Business Development Bank
IDB went as high as 10 per cent or more of the loan. I suggest to the minister that we will press him in committee to lay down some guidelines because I believe that one or more of these steps can be eliminated, thus reducing the cost to small businessmen.
In conclusion, we will ask that those who head this new organization be people who are not bankers per se, but people who are venturesome and innovative so that they may give through their counsel a new sense of hope and direction to this vital part of our society. Those are the remarks that I had planned on making on April 26, so at this point I will conclude, then whoever else is next on the list may continue the debate.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR INCORPORATION, OBJECTS, REGIONAL ADVISORY COUNCILS, POWERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on Bill C-20, the bill that will create the Federal Business Development Bank. I feel that it will be welcomed in British Columbia, especially in the fast growing areas such as the one in my riding of Okanagan Boundary where there are many small businesses which look after the needs of the people in the area as well as service the industries established with the aid of incentive grants which were provided a few years ago.
There are two apparent reasons for the need for this legislation in British Columbia. One is that British Columbia is one of the few provinces with no provincial plan to aid small businesses. The other is that there is a very limited area designated for DREE grants. The B.C. government is too busy buying into or establishing industrial enterprises to worry about small businesses. It is significant to note that one third of the business carried out by the Industrial Development Bank in the fiscal year 1973 was in British Columbia, involving 2,835 loans total-lying some $125 million. The reason for this is mainly that B.C. is one of the few provinces in Canada that does not have a provincial agency financing the activities of small businesses. The IDB has done a good job of assisting businessmen who cannot get help from chartered banks, but unfortunately they are restricted by the guidelines laid down in the act.
There are many areas of concern to small businesses. Small businesses play an important role in the economy, creating over 50 per cent of Canada's gross national product and paying 50 per cent of the taxes collected by the government. This is an important consideration to bear in mind if the government is to continue spending more and more money and employing more than 50 per cent of the people working in Canada. The small business is the breeding ground for new industries. What may be a small business today may well be a large industry tomorrow. Small businesses provide the means for entry into business of new entrepreneurial talent, and they are always striving to grow and to challenge large business. They provide a productive outlet for the energies of the large group of enterprising and independent people who attach great value to economic independence. They are often the most efficient form of business organization and are the reason many important trades and industries are made up mainly of small business. They add greatly to the variety of products and services offered to the consumers. The reason is that they can flourish in a limited or specialized

market, an activity which is not worthwhile for a larger business.
Many small businesses act as specialized suppliers to large companies for parts or components which can be produced at a lower cost than that of a larger company. The small businesses provide competition and checks and balances on the large corporations which are often inefficient, and so these small businesses contribute to the efficiency of the economic system as a whole.
Their major difficulty is their inability to obtain funds. Sometimes, for the want of a mere $5,000 to $10,000 they are forced to go under. The banks will not take the additional risk because they do not have the staff or are not willing to take the time to help the small business; neither do they have the expertise to understand the problems which small businessmen encounter. Often banks find that they can make more money on the large and safer account. Thus, they place their efforts in that direction and let the small business go under.
The Federal Business Development Bank can certainly do much to help these businessmen, provided it has the proper orientation to do so. Nowhere in this bill is preferential treatment given to Canadian-owned firms as opposed to those that may be controlled in a foreign land. What we are seeing is a shifting of the IDB from the Department of Finance to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. We have had some experience of the way in which the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) has run similar corporations in this country. I am referring to the Export Development Corporation. The minister has been quite willing to make loans to foreign governments for the benefit of the relatively large corporations in Canada, most of them more than 50 per cent foreign-owned. He has been willing to make those loans on a long-term basis at interest rates of approximately 7 per cent in contrast with the current interest rate at the IDB of 11 per cent, and for larger loans, of 12 per cent.
This brings to mind the time when the government found an excuse not to help the fruit industry in British Columbia under the export market development program. The fruit industry had a good program to put forward which would have given a great advantage to these Canadian producers. But when the chips were down and the industry asked for financial assistance, they could not obtain it. Therefore, they had to put up all the money themselves.
Another instance comes to mind of a small business in Summerland in my riding which had taken insurance against losses under the provisions of the Export Development Corporation. When this small business, which was doing as much as possible to employ people in Canada and use the product of the orchards of British Columbia, encountered a loss in its export trade, the corporation found a clause under which they denied this company's claim for losses. I believe that had this been a large company, probably 50 per cent foreign-owned, they would have been able to convince the Export Development Corporation that this claim should have been paid. However, because this was a small business, they did not have the resources to do this and thus had to take their losses. This
May 6, 1974

is an example of the attitude that the government takes toward the small businessman in this country.
The needs of Canadian businessmen are very simple, Canadian businessmen need relatively cheap money, and they would like less interference from government. They do not appreciate having to fill out the many forms they receive from all levels of government. They would certainly like to fill out fewer forms. They would like the amount of collateral required to obtain a loan reduced. They do not mind putting up collateral, but they do not want to be harassed by having to put up so much collateral that in the end the loan they get is almost meaningless.
I do not think they would mind getting advice on management from the new corporation, but it is important to realize that the small businessman already knows his needs. In most cases, there is no point in high priced executives telling him how to run his business. His real needs are relatively cheap funds, less government interference in forms to be filled out, and a competitive atmosphere in which he can continue to grow.
This bill appears to do no more than reconstitute the Industrial Development Bank and give certain other powers to the new corporation. Let us hope that the guidelines laid down by this bill will not be so restrictive. Let us hope that when the legislation is passed the organization set up under the Federal Business Development Bank is oriented to the needs of the businessman, and that he will get the help that he has been denied for many years. A strong business community will certainly do much to help Canada in its development and growth.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I merely wish to say a few words about that quite important bill since it contains provisions which would enable the small businesses of my area to take advantage of some financial incentives as well as the assistance of technicians and experts for the organization and the improvement of their businesses.
I understand that under this bill, a Federal Business Development Bank will be created. This legislation should be ratified and enforced as soon as possible so not to delay the development of rural areas where few benefits were granted in the past for such undertakings.
The Department of Regional Economic Expansion is already existing. Through various measures, businesses can obtain financial benefits, but considerable capital is too often required thus preventing promoters to take advantage of it precisely due to the lack of capital.
The Industrial Development Bank grants loans, but very carefully, and representations have often been made by business owners that they were experiencing great difficulty in having their applications accepted for loans which could help them expand, create jobs and be truly competitive.
In my area two community chests work in a quite extraordinary way. Local funds were raised. People investing in those community chests would like borrowers putting those funds to use to succeed in their undertaking.
Prairie Grain Payments Act
Now I see that a Federal Business Development Bank will complete the picture provided those institutions work together and supplement one another rather than tell applicants, go to the Industrial Development Bank, the community chest, the Caisse Populaire, the Provincial Bank or any other bank. I would like to see set up under this act regional advisory councils made up of responsible men, men very carefully chosen, in order to help those who still have enough initiative and courage left to set up new industries.
I often said in this House, and I repeat it again today, that whenever any government introduces legislation likely to help industrial development and small businesses in rural areas, I will support it immediately so that legislation can come into force. So for that reason I will limit my remarks to saying that I support the principle of this bill and I welcome this legislation. I hope that later we can improve it by amending it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ADVANCE PAYMENT
speechtext:
that Bill C-25, to amend the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-25 is another important step in the over-all program and policies of the government in trying to assure that prairie agriculture, that grain agriculture in Canada, is in a first rate position from the point of view of its operations, from the point of view of the business itself, and particularly from the point of view of the welfare and well being of the individuals involved in it.
Our over-all package of proposals, those either directly related to the Canadian Wheat Board or to the grain industry generally, and those being developed by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), are designed to assure that farmers do have a fair and adequate return on their work, for their families and for themselves. This has not always been the case. Indeed, farmers have gone through long periods of time when, instead of receiving a fair and adequate return per hour of work, they received far less than their fair share of the returns to all Canadians generated from the tremendous progress made in the economy throughout the country. It was only in fairly recent times that the producers of grain, particularly those who produce for export, experienced a change in their returns so that they have shared to some extent in the productivity increases which are common throughout many sectors of the economy, but which are especially noted in the field of agriculture.
In times past farmers saw year after year go by with very little improvement in their returns on any basis, and

May 6, 1974
Prairie Grain Payments Act
indeed struggled hard to see any improvement at all in the returns for their labour. They managed to exist where they could, partly by their own ingenuity and productivity, because they were willing to undertake whatever steps were necessary to produce more agricultural production during their hours of work, by seizing on technological change and putting it to work for the good of Canada and the good of the world.
In recent times an adjustment has taken place and we see grain prices giving farmers levels of returns which, in effect, do give them fairer treatment. I think it is important, as we look at this over-all situation, that we try to make the case as clearly as we can to all Canadians that a good deal of the change in price throughout the economy was due, and long overdue, to the farmers. In other words, to the extent that food price changes which result from a better return to farmers, have caused changes in price levels across the country, it should not be seen as part of the inflation which the negotiator, whether he be a doctor, lawyer or blue collar worker, tries to make up. A great deal of the adjustment which has taken place in favour of the grain producer is something which all of us ought to see as having been inevitable and necessary, and not something which we should get back.
The bill before us proposes two simple changes in the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act. In the first place, a change is made increasing the $6,000 limit to $15,000; in the second place, the change allows multiple granting of advances where more than one person engaged in the business of farming is joined in the same permit book and where it would be unfair for all of them to be treated as one farm.
If we look at the history of the legislation we can see how far we have come in a number of ways. The first grain advance payment was part of the program of the Conservatives when they came to power in 1957 under the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). It showed that they had some feeling for the needs of western Canada, in contrast with the attitude and approach of that party today which does not appreciate or see the needs of western Canada. Indeed, in contrast to the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert, the opposition leader does not have any appreciation of the nature of western farmers' problems.
In the 1957 bill certain cash advances were provided to farmers on their farm-stored grain for the first time. The maximum level prescribed in the bill was $3,000. We introduced legislation several years ago which changed that to the present limit of $6,000, and we are now proposing that it be increased to $15,000. This is a tremendous increase from the level of 1957.
In 1957, the per bushel advance possible was a mere 50 cents per bushel of wheat, 20 cents per bushel of oats and 35 cents per bushel of barley. Two years ago, we changed that to $1 per bushel of wheat, 40 cents per bushel of oats and 70 cents per bushel of barley. At the present time, in the elevators across the prairies, farmers with the $6,000 limit are entitled to advances of $1.50 per bushel of wheat, 70 cents per bushel of oats and 90 cents per bushel of barley. The increase from 50 cents to $1.50 for wheat

reflects the changed economic circumstances, but also reflects our efforts to try to make the cash advance legislation fit the special circumstances of farmers.
We now have a system by which the farmer can receive his cash in advance of delivery in relation to the kind of delivery opportunity he is going to be given for his grain during the year. It is not, therefore, an interference in the encouragement of production or market forces working upon them, but it is an advance to him of money which he would receive otherwise when he delivers his grain. Because grain is such an easily stored commodity and the farmers involved in the program are so reliable, the program has worked extremely well. There are few programs involving as many hundreds of millions of dollars in advances and involving up to 200,000 producers which have the proud record of this one in terms of minimum of default and minimum of abuse. The producers can be trusted, the security of grain is there, and therefore money can be advanced to them ahead of actual delivery opportunity.
The key in this is that farmers are relieved of some of the distress which can on occasion occur. Although they have the grain and appear to have wealth to sustain them, they do not have delivery opportunities so have to find some other means, either borrowing money or selling grain at a low price in a local market, in order to obtain cash. It is this last point which is important in our discussion today. We do not want to see any unnecessary pressure on the producer to dispose of grain in one market because he cannot wait for quotas. It is in this connection that this particular change is introduced. We foresee a market in feed grains for domestic purposes which is less restrictive than at the present time because of the over-all need to have feed grains prices which are equitable across the country. Producers of animal products who have to buy feed grains as part of their cost of operation will be on an equal footing, separated only by what naturally separates them, geographical facts and the cost of moving products from one place to another.
In that connection the great bulk of grains delivered by farmers for commercial purposes in western Canada will continue to be delivered to the Canadian Wheat Board with delivery opportunity arranged as equitably as possible among producers. The great bulk of farmers will therefore have exactly the same choice that they have now to deliver to the Canadian Wheat Board on quotas as those quotas become available. There will be some who may choose, as they do now, to deliver to their own animals, to neighbours feeding animals or to neighbours slightly further away.
What we would like to assure is that those who want to hold their grain in order to deliver it on quotas are not forced to deliver in another manner because of any desperate need for cash in advance of their delivery opportunity. The cash advance legislation provides this kind of assurance. By its existence the farmer who has grain and who will have quotas throughout the year to deliver his wheat, oats or barley, can receive from the Canadian Wheat Board the greater proportion of his cash at the time he needs it in advance of that delivery opportunity being made available.
May 6, 1974

We see this bill as continuing the tremendous advantage of obtaining cash in advance of delivery opportunity, as having specific application to the feed grains proposal, and assuring that there will be equitable pricing of grain across the country. I commend it to hon. members in this House. Just as in 1957 it demonstrated the kind of understanding and interest in western agriculture which the right hon. member for Prince Albert has always shown, so today it carries the commitment of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) toward understanding and improving conditions in western Canada. The present Prime Minister committed this government to bringing in tremendous changes in western Canada. He committed the government to end discrimination in freight rates and to bring about diversified economic growth in western Canada. He committed the government to a new national policy which will take into account the aspirations of western Canada.
When the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert was prime minister, it was easy for him to be aware of the problems of prairie farmers and attempt to do something about them. He was a Saskatchewan man. He had lived for a long time in that part of the country; he had heard the problems of the area discussed in the press and elsewhere, and obviously wanted to do something about the problems of the area. It is that much more impressive that the present Prime Minister, in determining to come to grips with the problems of western Canada, made sure he understood the problems of the west, although he comes from an area of the country different from that from which the right hon. member for Prince Albert comes.
This prairie grain advance payments legislation, which is but one forward step being taken, is a further demonstration of the determination of this government, as expressed in the Western Economic Opportunities Conference, to leave no section of this country unattended, and to leave no section of the country feeling that its aspirations are being neglected. This legislation, therefore, is part of our commitment to meet the aspirations of western Canada. We are trying to change the national concept laid down by Sir John A. Macdonald under which the country was supposed to consist of hewers of wood and drawers of water. We are trying to decentralize the operations of government in the way witnessed in recent months by establishing, for instance, key offices of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion in Saskatoon, in Moncton and in other areas.
This bill is a small but important step on the course about which the Prime Minister has spoken, a course which is strongly espoused within the Liberal party, a course, namely, which suggests that the government of this country must understand each area of this country, and each one of us, no matter from which part of the country he comes-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister responsible for the Wheat Board treated the House to another of his lectures. Everything seemed to go quite well until he tried to inject humour at the end of his speech. He tried to tell us what the government has done to meet the problems of western Canada. If he wants to retain credi-
2066

May 6, 1974
Prairie Grain Payments Act
bility, he should examine carefully what he said in the closing minutes of his speech.
The minister said that grain farmers are now getting fair and adequate returns, that western grain producers at last are receiving the sorts of returns they have not received for the last few years. That situation is reflected throughout the whole of the economy of Canada, and not just in the economy of western Canada.
When considering what this bill does, we must look beyond the aspect of cash advances to prairie farmers and others and consider the agriculture industry in total. Grain farming is one of the foundations on which our agriculture industry is built. It is my impression that the agriculture industry is in a state of confusion it has not known for many years. This is borne out by the legitimate and well intentioned questions asked every day in this House on the subjects of hogs, livestock, poultry and government policy in these areas.
Bill C-25 is only a small step forward, granted, but it should be welcome. It provides for an increase in cash advances. The bill has nothing new or different to say about agriculture; actually, it is long overdue. It should have been introduced much earlier. Basically, the legislation proposes an increase in the cash advance with respect to farm-stored grain from $6,000 to $15,000 where one person is concerned, to $30,000 where two people or a partnership are involved, and to a maximum of $45,000 where a company or three people are concerned.
These increases are certainly justified in the light of farmers' needs. Indeed, they are long overdue. We have seen the cost of seed, fertilizer, barbed wire, bailer twine, chemicals, machinery and a host of other articles or commodities used on the farm go up by amounts which range from 20 per cent to as high as 200 per cent. The new ceilings governing cash advances are welcome, since they are based on realistic considerations.
At the present time we enjoy a relatively high price for grain and it appears as though prices will continue to be relatively high for the next few years, though possibly not as high as they are today. Thank God this is the case, because otherwise with this government's track record, we might be seeing another operation LIFT. As we move into the summer and toward the prospect of a general election, there is still no sign from the government as to what farmers may expect by way of a comprehensive agricultural policy. There is still no indication of the direction in which agriculture is expected to move. We hear muttering and hints, but that is all.
About a month ago, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) was going around the country saying that if he had his way he would take over the job of the minister responsible for the Wheat Board because he felt he could operate more effectively if both portfolios were combined. The results of this uncertainty are being felt by agriculture producers all across Canada. For too long the government has reminded us of a ship lurching first in one direction and then in another, with no one in command, no one with a sense of leadership. There have been indications for some time that a move is to be made toward stabilization, but this has not gone beyond occasional

references in speeches by the minister and some of his colleagues. To what extent does the government propose to intervene, if at all? What does the government have in mind by stabilization? Would any scheme which it might produce be a necessary one at the present time? These are questions which should be dealt with in the context of any bill dealing with cash advances or assistance to agriculture generally.
The minister responsible for the Wheat Board has taken his usual arrogant approach to these issues. He still gives the impression he has all the answers. He likes to tell the farmers, members of the opposition and any others who will listen what will be done. I say to him that he may be able to write intellectually stimulating notes to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) but that he leaves most of the farmers in western Canada cold.
As I say, it is a good thing that grain prices are relatively high. Nevertheless, the situation should be viewed in the light of the total agriculture picture, and the industry as a whole has nothing on which to plan its operations for the next few years. I have here a report of a statement made by Mr. Bill Stewart, the minister of agriculture in Ontario. It says:
Agriculture Minister William Stewart said Ontario has urged the federal government to immediately increase the producer prices of butter and skim milk powder by two cents a pound. He told the Legislature on April 25 the current federal dairy policy doesn't go far enough in providing the incentive to maintain and increase industrial milk production.
This illustrates what I have been saying about the lack of leadership on the part of the government, or its agriculture spokesmen. The beef subsidy was implemented hastily without regard for its effect on the marketplace. For a while, it caused chaos, and now it appears the beef industry is in full retreat as a result of actions which compounded earlier damage done by this administration.
I turn, now, to the government's feed grain policy. The Minister of Agriculture and the minister responsible for the Wheat Board said it was the fairest policy they could devise. That is a lot of rubbish and they must know it is not the case. The policy -vas devised as a political half-way measure. Because of the difficulty which arises in relation to the monitoring aspect, the system of payments has not worked since the program was introduced. One of the indications of the government's lack of vision is the quantity of corn imported into Canada from the United States as a result of the unrealistic pricing of domestic feed grain.
The damage done by the federal government in the application of this interim policy, compounded by antics on the part of certain provincial governments, has led to nothing short of economic stagnation for the section of the industry engaged in animal production. Grain prices have risen so rapidly that the economics of producing milk and meat have completely changed in the matter of a few months. In addition to the confusion and uncertainty caused by the feed grain policy, the price maintenance effect must be taken into consideration. Domestic feed grain costs are being deliberately held up at a time when the last thing that is needed is a maintained minimum price.
May 6, 1974

I see that the minister responsible for the Wheat Board has left the chamber. I hope he will come back to listen to some of the remainder of the debate. If he decides not to do so, it will reinforce my comments about the arrogance displayed by the hon. gentleman from Saskatchewan.
What we need is the only kind of workable policy, a policy based on true supply and demand requirements. As I mentioned before, a political halfway measure will not work, is not working, and I think is a true demonstration to all parties of the House that it cannot work. Political halfway measures only complicate the issue, and if introduced into this House in another form I believe will not receive the support necessary for their passage.
Another area of concern in the question of feed grain is the seeming inability of the government to make up its mind on bringing forward a new policy in plenty of time for the political parties in this House, producer groups across the country and for provincial governments, particularly in Western Canada, to have a good look at the legislation to see whether or not it is acceptable. The debate on the feed grain issue has been going on for far too long. The government should act, and should act as soon as possible, to bring the matter before the public so it can be discussed in concrete terms.
So far as a grain policy is concerned, I think it is safe to say that Canada has almost reached the crossroads at this particular point in time. In my opinion we can opt for one of two policies. We can either opt for a policy that directs us toward a complete grain economy, which seems to be the policy we are adopting now; or we can direct our energies toward devising agricultural policies that provide for a grain-livestock economy, in which for the most part we feed and process our livestock in Canada and, if at all possible, ship the processed product to other parts of the world.
I know it is safe to say that it is the opinion of the Conservative party that the latter direction is the only acceptable one to follow so far as agricultural policy in Canada is concerned. I think we view with a certain amount of alarm the kind of situation that has developed in the production of hogs, livestock, eggs, turkeys, broilers. We seem to be driving ourselves into a strict grain economy and letting the United States produce the poultry products. I suggest that is a policy that is certainly unacceptable.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, it must be remembered by consumers that the only basic method that we have in Canada of reducing relatively high food costs is to increase domestic agricultural production. The public generally must realize that the farmers are entitled to, and indeed must be able to receive, a reasonable return on their time, effort and investment. The alternative to production at a profit is reduced production and increased imports, which ultimately will result in higher food costs for consumers. I say this, Mr. Speaker, because I believe it ties all our thoughts and goals together and points us in the direction we want to follow. While welcoming the amendment the government has brought forward to the cash advances legislation, I have no faith

House of Commons-that the government will give any meaningful, long-term direction to agriculture today.

Mr. Speaker, the minister gave us some advance warning that finally he was going to bring some legislation into this House, for on Friday last he issued a whole clutch of news releases. I did not know which was going to come first in his plans, an election or some legislation. This House has been in session during this 29th parliament for close to two years, during which time the minister has changed the direction of the marketing practices of the Canadian Wheat Board for domestic grain, practically without the benefit of legislation. Now that the government stands on the edge of defeat because of its mismanagement of Canadian affairs, its unwillingness to meet the problems of Canadians resulting from the cost of living, and its high-handed action in regard to grain marketing, the government finally brings in some legislation to double the amount of cash advance to farmers in the event that they cannot sell their grain.
Are we being given a preview of the minister's thinking? Is the minister concerned for our future grain sales to the extent that at this point in time he doubles cash advances? Let us remember that this was a measure introduced by a Conservative government, as the minister himself has mentioned, and introduced at a time when grain sales were at a very low ebb. The measure was designed to give some cash flow relief to farmers who at that time were unable to sell enough grain to keep themselves in business.
I wondered why the minister put emphasis on this measure at this time, so I looked at the report in the "Grain Statistics Weekly" put out by the Canadian Grain Commission. In terms of commercial disappearance of domestic and export grain at this point in time, our wheat sales are something over 117 million bushels less than the same time last year. And this, Mr. Speaker, in a crop year that has seen one of the highest world demands and market opportunities for wheat for many a year. The least the minister could have done when he introduced this bill was to explain why, with market conditions as they are at this point in time and with less than three months to the end of the crop year, we are over 117 million bushels short of the sales performance of the Canadian Wheat Board one year ago. That is the result of the minister monkeying around with what was a perfectly good marketing system. He armed himself with a monkey-wrench, a pair of plyers and a bale of haywire and started to work on the marketing machinery. That is the situation we are dealing with now, and primary marketings from farmers are almost in tune with the drop in export sales.
It was in these circumstances that the minister put out a bunch of press releases on Friday in respect of grain stabilization, a farm income package, cash advances, two-price wheat legislation and methods to bring certainty into the timing of final payments and so on. If he gets that all before the House at least maybe there will be some legislative base to work on.
In dealing with this bill I should like to point out one or two things to the House and perhaps to the minister. The

original bill was put in at a time when there was some difficulty with marketing. This kind of legislation depends on two or three basic assumptions, or two or three basic things being in place in the grain marketing industry, without which it will not work. It depends on a quota system that works, and this is pretty important because it is on the basis of a working quota system that a farmer is able to deliver his grain in an orderly fashion, and that the Canadian Wheat Board is sure that repayments can be made. This depends on a price system that works and one that is predictable so the farmer and the Canadian Wheat Board can have confidence in it.
What is the quota system to be in the coming crop year? We just do not know what it is to be. The other day I asked Mr. Jarvis, a witness who appeared before the committee, this question about pricing and the quota system, and he said we would have to wait for another month or two. He is one of the members of the minister's grains group, and that was his answer. How does the minister expect us to be happy with what he is proposing in terms of cash advances when he does not tell us what other packages of goodies he has in his pockets? We do not know what the pricing system is to be. I think the minister has in reality said that the system of pricing on August 1 is to be the Winnipeg commodity exchange. That is what he has been saying to this House, but he has not been able to come out and tell the farmers exactly what he intends to do. Can he not bear to contemplate the results of his handiwork? Are the results going to be so horrible that he will no t be able to contemplate them? Why does he not say what he is going to do? Does he not have the nerve to do so?

He better do so soon. When the cash advance legislation was passed, it was predicated and dependent upon a stable pricing system. Whatever benefits can be claimed for commodity marketing systems such as the Winnipeg Grain Exchange, stability is not one of them. Some people claim they can make more money this way, but you cannot claim stability. How can we have a cash advance system operating when we do not have a stable pricing and quota system? What will be the effect of the present suggested pricing system? How is the cash advance system going to work when it is dependent upon a monitoring system which is now being used to establish prices of feed grains on the prairies? If the farmers borrow these large amounts of money as envisaged by these amendments, and then either through the commodity exchange system or, by the present monitoring system the minister is using, prices drop disastrously, how are the farmers going to repay those cash advances proposed under this legislation?
I think the minister should explain these things instead of giving us a eulogy in his best classroom manner at the end of his speech, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta). I think the hon. member's point was well taken. It is nice to have a euphoric dream, and it is nice to have fine words, but what we must know is what the legislation is going to do. Will the Canadian Wheat Board be able to demand payments when the quota and pricing systems of the Canadian Wheat Board are no longer working and are no longer in place? How is one

going to demand payment from the farmer when quotas are not orderly or properly established? How is this all going to operate? How can you demand payment from the farmer when the bloc system, which was developed and working well, is practically destroyed? In view of the various experiments the minister is carrying out around the country, how can payment be fairly demanded from the farmer who is left in the position that he either cannot deliver the grain or the price has dropped so far down it is virtually impossible for him to repay his loans? Those are the questions that should be answered by the minister.
Perhaps the minister does not know the answers to these questions. Let me remind him that in 1971 and 1972 farmers were badgered for payments. They were suffering the miseries of persecution and dunning for payments. They could not deliver their grain and therefore could not get the money to pay the amounts they owed on their loans at that time. It is fine for the minister to stand in his place and blandly refer to the good record of payments on the part of the farmers, and that the farmers can be trusted, but I have some serious doubts as to whether we can trust the minister.

Yes. The other day we heard demands in respect of the Unemployment Insurance Commission that the board of referees be bilingual. I told them that the language ought to be Russian or some other ethnic language because that would be a lot better in Saskatchewan. However, these are some of the policies the minister trots out. The Livestock Feed Board may even ask the Wheat Board to sell feed grains in the domestic market and cut off their export sales which have already been made. One reason we have this very poor export performance is this type of approach. Then the experts go on to say that in the next crop year if the Canadian Wheat Board does sell grain in the domestic market the only way they can establish a price is through the Winnipeg commodity exchange. This is the story that is told by newsmen on the CBC. This is the type of policy that is being worked out. Western feed grain will be bought and sold freely and not restricted to any quantity.
I got a kick out of hearing the minister say that they will be selling it to their neighbours but that their neighbours may be a fair piece away. I thought that was pretty good. This is the sort of program that is being proposed. It is the type of program we must consider in respect of this legislation. I think there are two responsibilities here with regard to this legislation. One is to see that it will operate in such a way that if the producer borrows the money he will have full expectation of being able to repay it by the only method he has, which is the delivery of grain. I think the other responsibility we have is to the taxpayer of Canada who is making the money available on an interest-free basis. These are the two responsibilities members of this House have. Perhaps a third responsibility is to see that the farmer can function in good times and in bad times without too much duress.
The point I should like to make is that if the minister intends to change the operations of the Canadian Wheat Board to the extent they have already been changed and to the extent they are apparently to be changed, then the farmer will not be in a position in which he can be sure he will be able to repay the money and the Canadian Wheat
Prairie Grain Payments Act
Board will not be in a position in which it can be sure that it can recover these payments due. My real fear is that this program which has been excellent, and which has served the people of Canada and the farmers very well, will come into disrepute. That is the real danger. When the minister stood up he made no attempt to tell the House how this legislation could work well under the new pricing and selling methods which will be used in respect of feed grain sales. We must not forget that feed wheat is an integral part of the industry.
This is not only a concern of mine. Other people share this concern, including the government of Manitoba. The minister of agriculture of that province even went to the extent of polling the farmers of Manitoba in order to find out their attitude concerning feed grain marketing. The federal Minister of Agriculture undoubtedly has received opinions from such organizations as the Federation of Agriculture, the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool and the National Farmer's Union. I am sure they told him the same things they told me. They are very concerned about the path he is taking particularly with regard to domestic grain. I am sure they expressed that concern to him as it has been expressed in this House. The minister has chosen to ignore entirely these expressions of concern.
The minister goes on his merry way and winds up making a peroration about what a nice thing it will be when all Canadians lives together in a happy community where momma loves poppa, poppa loves momma and the kids love everybody. That is the sort of dreamland in which the minister is living, but the ordinary producer and farmer must live in the real world where he has not only to borrow money but to repay it. We have not had the answers this afternoon, so I suppose we will not get them. I hope the minister will tell the railroads that branch lines will be in operation soon. It is our hope that he will get them going by June 1.
